# Exploratory Factor Analysis {#sec-efa} Many constructs in education research, such as anxiety, motivation, or engagement, cannot be measured directly. Instead, we measure them with sets of survey items. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) asks how many underlying dimensions (*factors*) explain the correlations among a set of items, and which items go with which factor. In this chapter, we start with reliability (Cronbach's alpha) for a single subscale. Then we use EFA to explore the structure of a full questionnaire. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(haven) library(psych) library(corrplot) ``` ::: ## The data We use the SPSS Anxiety Questionnaire (SAQ) from Andy Field's *Discovering Statistics Using SPSS*. It has 23 items about anxiety related to statistics, computers, and mathematics, completed by 2,571 students. Each item is rated from 1 (strongly agree) to 5 (strongly disagree). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} saq <- read_dta("data/saq.dta") glimpse(saq) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 2,571 Columns: 23 $ Q01 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1,… $ Q02 1, 1, 3, 1, 1, 1, 3, 2, 3, 4, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2,… $ Q03 4, 4, 2, 1, 3, 3, 3, 3, 1, 4, 5, 3, 3, 1, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4, 1, 3,… $ Q04 2, 3, 2, 4, 2, 2, 2, 2, 4, 3, 2, 3, 4, 2, 4, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2,… $ Q05 2, 2, 4, 3, 2, 4, 2, 2, 5, 2, 2, 4, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 3, 3, 3, 4,… $ Q06 2, 2, 1, 3, 3, 4, 2, 2, 3, 1, 1, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 4, 1, 4, 1,… $ Q07 3, 2, 2, 4, 3, 4, 2, 2, 5, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 1, 3, 1, 4, 2,… $ Q08 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 5, 2, 2, 1, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1,… $ Q09 1, 5, 2, 2, 4, 4, 3, 4, 3, 3, 5, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 1,… $ Q10 2, 2, 2, 4, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1,… $ Q11 1, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 5, 2, 1, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1,… $ Q12 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 5, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, 5, 4,… $ Q13 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 5, 2, 1, 2, 4, 2, 2, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1,… $ Q14 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 5, 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 3, 3, 1, 3, 2, 5, 1,… $ Q15 2, 4, 2, 3, 2, 5, 2, 3, 5, 2, 1, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1, 4, 2, 5, 1,… $ Q16 3, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 5, 3, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 3, 2, 3, 3, 5, 2,… $ Q17 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 5, 2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1,… $ Q18 2, 2, 3, 4, 3, 5, 2, 2, 5, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 3, 3, 1, 2, 1, 5, 1,… $ Q19 3, 3, 1, 2, 3, 1, 3, 4, 2, 3, 5, 3, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 2, 4, 1, 2,… $ Q20 2, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 2, 3, 5, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 4, 3, 2, 3, 2, 5, 4,… $ Q21 2, 4, 3, 4, 2, 3, 2, 2, 5, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 4, 2, 1, 3, 2, 5, 3,… $ Q22 2, 4, 2, 4, 4, 1, 4, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 3, 3, 4, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 2,… $ Q23 5, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4, 4, 1, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5,… ``` ::: ::: ### Reverse coding Most items are worded so that agreeing indicates more anxiety (for example, Q01: "Statistics makes me cry"). Q03, "Standard deviations excite me," is worded in the opposite direction. A correlation plot shows the problem: Q03 correlates negatively with most of the other items. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cor(saq) |> corrplot(method = "color", type = "upper", tl.cex = 0.7) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](09-efa_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: We reverse-code Q03 by subtracting it from 6 (one more than the highest response) and drop the original: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} saq_clean <- saq |> mutate(Q03R = 6 - Q03) |> select(-Q03) ``` ::: ## Reliability ### Cronbach's alpha Seven items ask about computers (Q06, Q07, Q10, Q13, Q14, Q15, and Q18). If we plan to combine them into a subscale, we should first check that they hang together. Cronbach's alpha is the most common index of internal consistency. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} computers <- saq_clean |> select(Q06, Q07, Q10, Q13, Q14, Q15, Q18) psych::alpha(computers) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reliability analysis Call: psych::alpha(x = computers) raw_alpha std.alpha G6(smc) average_r S/N ase mean sd median_r 0.82 0.82 0.81 0.4 4.6 0.0052 2.6 0.71 0.39 95% confidence boundaries lower alpha upper Feldt 0.81 0.82 0.83 Duhachek 0.81 0.82 0.83 Reliability if an item is dropped: raw_alpha std.alpha G6(smc) average_r S/N alpha se var.r med.r Q06 0.79 0.79 0.77 0.38 3.7 0.0063 0.0081 0.38 Q07 0.79 0.79 0.77 0.38 3.7 0.0063 0.0079 0.36 Q10 0.82 0.82 0.80 0.44 4.7 0.0053 0.0043 0.44 Q13 0.79 0.79 0.77 0.39 3.8 0.0062 0.0081 0.38 Q14 0.80 0.80 0.77 0.39 3.9 0.0060 0.0085 0.36 Q15 0.81 0.81 0.79 0.41 4.2 0.0056 0.0095 0.44 Q18 0.79 0.78 0.76 0.38 3.6 0.0064 0.0058 0.38 Item statistics n raw.r std.r r.cor r.drop mean sd Q06 2571 0.75 0.74 0.68 0.62 2.2 1.12 Q07 2571 0.75 0.73 0.68 0.62 2.9 1.10 Q10 2571 0.54 0.57 0.44 0.40 2.3 0.88 Q13 2571 0.72 0.73 0.67 0.61 2.4 0.95 Q14 2571 0.70 0.70 0.64 0.58 2.9 1.00 Q15 2571 0.64 0.64 0.54 0.49 2.8 1.01 Q18 2571 0.76 0.76 0.72 0.65 2.6 1.05 Non missing response frequency for each item 1 2 3 4 5 miss Q06 0.27 0.44 0.13 0.10 0.06 0 Q07 0.07 0.34 0.26 0.24 0.09 0 Q10 0.14 0.57 0.18 0.10 0.02 0 Q13 0.12 0.48 0.25 0.12 0.03 0 Q14 0.06 0.31 0.38 0.18 0.07 0 Q15 0.07 0.39 0.30 0.18 0.06 0 Q18 0.14 0.37 0.31 0.12 0.06 0 ``` ::: ::: We write `psych::alpha()` to make sure R uses the `alpha()` function from `psych`, since other packages have functions with the same name. The raw alpha of 0.82 suggests good internal consistency. Values of 0.70 or higher are usually considered acceptable. The "Reliability if an item is dropped" table shows what alpha would be without each item. If dropping an item would *raise* alpha, that item may not fit the scale well. ### Adding an item that does not fit What happens if we add Q23, "If I'm good at statistics my friends will think I'm a nerd"? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} computers2 <- saq_clean |> select(Q06, Q07, Q10, Q13, Q14, Q15, Q18, Q23) psych::alpha(computers2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Some items ( Q23 ) were negatively correlated with the first principal component and probably should be reversed. To do this, run the function again with the 'check.keys=TRUE' option ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reliability analysis Call: psych::alpha(x = computers2) raw_alpha std.alpha G6(smc) average_r S/N ase mean sd median_r 0.76 0.76 0.76 0.28 3.1 0.0068 2.7 0.62 0.34 95% confidence boundaries lower alpha upper Feldt 0.74 0.76 0.77 Duhachek 0.74 0.76 0.77 Reliability if an item is dropped: raw_alpha std.alpha G6(smc) average_r S/N alpha se var.r med.r Q06 0.70 0.71 0.71 0.26 2.4 0.0085 0.0483 0.30 Q07 0.70 0.71 0.71 0.26 2.4 0.0085 0.0482 0.32 Q10 0.74 0.75 0.75 0.29 2.9 0.0073 0.0571 0.39 Q13 0.71 0.71 0.72 0.26 2.4 0.0083 0.0493 0.32 Q14 0.71 0.71 0.72 0.26 2.5 0.0082 0.0512 0.32 Q15 0.73 0.73 0.74 0.28 2.7 0.0077 0.0556 0.32 Q18 0.70 0.70 0.71 0.25 2.4 0.0086 0.0450 0.32 Q23 0.82 0.82 0.81 0.40 4.6 0.0052 0.0077 0.39 Item statistics n raw.r std.r r.cor r.drop mean sd Q06 2571 0.73 0.72 0.68 0.597 2.2 1.12 Q07 2571 0.73 0.72 0.68 0.597 2.9 1.10 Q10 2571 0.53 0.55 0.44 0.383 2.3 0.88 Q13 2571 0.71 0.71 0.67 0.590 2.4 0.95 Q14 2571 0.69 0.69 0.64 0.562 2.9 1.00 Q15 2571 0.62 0.63 0.54 0.473 2.8 1.01 Q18 2571 0.74 0.74 0.72 0.622 2.6 1.05 Q23 2571 0.12 0.11 -0.10 -0.092 3.4 1.04 Non missing response frequency for each item 1 2 3 4 5 miss Q06 0.27 0.44 0.13 0.10 0.06 0 Q07 0.07 0.34 0.26 0.24 0.09 0 Q10 0.14 0.57 0.18 0.10 0.02 0 Q13 0.12 0.48 0.25 0.12 0.03 0 Q14 0.06 0.31 0.38 0.18 0.07 0 Q15 0.07 0.39 0.30 0.18 0.06 0 Q18 0.14 0.37 0.31 0.12 0.06 0 Q23 0.06 0.12 0.27 0.42 0.12 0 ``` ::: ::: Alpha drops to 0.76, and `psych` warns that Q23 is negatively correlated with the rest of the scale. The item-dropped table confirms that removing Q23 would restore alpha to 0.82. ### Creating a scale score Once we are satisfied with a subscale, `scoreItems()` computes each student's mean across its items: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} keys <- list(computers = c("Q06", "Q07", "Q10", "Q13", "Q14", "Q15", "Q18")) scales <- scoreItems(keys, saq_clean, totals = FALSE) saq_scored <- saq_clean |> bind_cols(as_tibble(scales$scores)) describe(saq_scored$computers) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Exploratory factor analysis Alpha tells us whether a set of items is internally consistent. It does not tell us whether the items measure one construct or several. For that, we turn to EFA. ### Are the data suitable? Two checks tell us whether the items are correlated enough for factor analysis. The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy ranges from 0 to 1. Values above 0.80 are generally considered good. Bartlett's test of sphericity tests whether the correlation matrix differs from an identity matrix (no correlations at all). A significant result is what we want. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} KMO(saq_clean)$MSA ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0.9302245 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cortest.bartlett(cor(saq_clean), n = nrow(saq_clean)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $chisq [1] 19334.49 $p.value [1] 0 $df [1] 253 ``` ::: ::: The KMO is 0.93, and Bartlett's test is significant. Both suggest the data are suitable for factor analysis. ### How many factors? The most important decision in EFA is how many factors to retain. Several aids are available: - **Kaiser's rule**: retain components with eigenvalues greater than 1. - **The scree plot**: retain the factors before the plot levels off. - **Parallel analysis**: retain factors whose eigenvalues are larger than those from random data of the same size. This is generally the most accurate of the three. `fa.parallel()` draws a scree plot with parallel analysis results for both principal components (`PC`) and factors (`FA`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(663) fa.parallel(saq_clean, fm = "pa", fa = "both") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](09-efa_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Parallel analysis suggests that the number of factors = 7 and the number of components = 4 ``` ::: ::: The aids do not agree perfectly. Parallel analysis suggests six factors, but four components. Four principal components also have eigenvalues greater than 1. Because two of the guides point to four, and because the item content covers four themes (statistics, computers, mathematics, and peers), we retain four. In your own work, the decision should weigh these statistical aids alongside theory and interpretability. ### Extracting the factors `fa()` fits the factor model. We use principal axis factoring (`fm = "pa"`), a common extraction method that does not assume multivariate normality. We start without rotation: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} efa_unrotated <- fa(saq_clean, nfactors = 4, rotate = "none", fm = "pa") print(efa_unrotated$loadings, cutoff = 0.3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Loadings: PA1 PA2 PA3 PA4 Q01 0.557 Q02 0.372 Q04 0.607 Q05 0.522 Q06 0.552 0.488 Q07 0.663 Q08 0.546 0.482 Q09 0.460 Q10 0.404 Q11 0.646 0.313 Q12 0.643 Q13 0.650 Q14 0.628 Q15 0.559 Q16 0.653 Q17 0.632 0.359 Q18 0.684 Q19 -0.397 Q20 0.407 Q21 0.633 Q22 Q23 Q03R 0.605 PA1 PA2 PA3 PA4 SS loadings 6.744 1.127 0.814 0.624 Proportion Var 0.293 0.049 0.035 0.027 Cumulative Var 0.293 0.342 0.378 0.405 ``` ::: ::: A *loading* is the correlation between an item and a factor. We hide loadings below 0.3 to make the pattern easier to read. In the unrotated solution, nearly every item loads on the first factor. This is typical: unrotated factor analysis extracts as much variance as possible into the first factor, which makes the solution hard to interpret. ### Rotation Rotation redistributes the variance across factors to approach *simple structure*, in which each item loads strongly on one factor and weakly on the others. Rotation does not change how well the model fits. It changes only how the variance is divided among the factors. There are two families of rotation: - **Orthogonal** rotations (such as varimax) keep the factors uncorrelated. - **Oblique** rotations (such as promax) allow the factors to correlate. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} efa_varimax <- fa(saq_clean, nfactors = 4, rotate = "varimax", fm = "pa") print(efa_varimax$loadings, cutoff = 0.3, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Loadings: PA1 PA3 PA4 PA2 Q01 0.504 Q04 0.527 Q12 0.510 0.398 Q16 0.543 Q21 0.594 Q03R 0.505 0.399 Q06 0.752 Q07 0.364 0.559 Q13 0.564 Q18 0.366 0.612 Q08 0.759 Q11 0.688 Q17 0.641 Q09 -0.559 Q02 -0.464 Q05 0.436 Q10 0.380 Q14 0.388 0.485 Q15 0.377 Q19 -0.375 Q20 0.465 Q22 -0.465 Q23 -0.329 PA1 PA3 PA4 PA2 SS loadings 3.034 2.854 1.986 1.435 Proportion Var 0.132 0.124 0.086 0.062 Cumulative Var 0.132 0.256 0.342 0.405 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} efa_promax <- fa(saq_clean, nfactors = 4, rotate = "promax", fm = "pa") print(efa_promax$loadings, cutoff = 0.3, sort = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Loadings: PA1 PA3 PA4 PA2 Q01 0.559 Q04 0.566 Q12 0.508 Q16 0.567 Q20 0.582 Q21 0.669 Q03R 0.530 Q06 0.961 Q07 0.550 Q13 0.566 Q18 0.630 Q08 0.839 Q11 0.717 Q17 0.643 Q09 0.565 Q02 0.450 Q05 0.454 Q10 0.405 Q14 0.444 Q15 0.302 Q19 0.323 Q22 0.480 Q23 0.363 PA1 PA3 PA4 PA2 SS loadings 2.956 2.589 1.753 1.162 Proportion Var 0.129 0.113 0.076 0.051 Cumulative Var 0.129 0.241 0.317 0.368 ``` ::: ::: In both rotated solutions, the items sort into four groups. With promax, each item loads on only one factor, which is closer to simple structure. The four factors appear to correspond to: - fear of statistics (PA1) - fear of computers (PA3) - fear of mathematics (PA4) - fear of negative evaluation from peers (PA2) The promax solution also estimates the correlations among the factors: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(efa_promax$Phi, 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` PA1 PA3 PA4 PA2 PA1 1.00 0.68 0.55 -0.44 PA3 0.68 1.00 0.58 -0.37 PA4 0.55 0.58 1.00 -0.20 PA2 -0.44 -0.37 -0.20 1.00 ``` ::: ::: Several factors correlate at 0.5 or higher. In most social science settings, we would expect related constructs like these to be correlated. This suggests that an oblique rotation is the more realistic choice here. `fa.diagram()` shows the promax solution as a path diagram: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fa.diagram(efa_promax) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](09-efa_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Factor scores Finally, we can estimate each student's score on each factor: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} factor_scores <- as_tibble(efa_promax$scores) glimpse(factor_scores) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 2,571 Columns: 4 $ PA1 -1.13514544, -0.42373326, 0.09474844, 0.70888719, -0.75336336, 0.2… $ PA3 -0.656897900, -0.569933489, -0.337264493, 0.585706832, -0.01731724… $ PA4 -1.53016147, -0.38297269, -0.03502744, -0.23964113, -0.42449977, 0… $ PA2 -0.10078520, 0.59963412, -0.63254390, -0.45306944, 0.56114971, -0.… ``` ::: ::: These scores can be used in later analyses, much like the scale score we created with `scoreItems()`. @sec-cfa takes the next step: testing whether a hypothesized factor structure fits the data.
